examples.problem_statement: Convert 1/7 to decimal form and analyze its repeating pattern and underlying geometric progression.

solution.description: Set the problem up as the division of 1 by 7. Converting the fraction means carrying that division past the decimal point until the digits start to repeat.
Place the decimal point and bring down a zero, making 10. Seven goes into 10 once, so the first decimal digit is 1 and a remainder of 3 is left to carry on with.
Attach a zero to the remainder 3 to make 30. Seven fours are 28, so the next digit is 4 and the remainder becomes 2; the quotient now reads 0.14.
Attach a zero to the 2 to make 20. Seven twos are 14, giving the digit 2 and a remainder of 6, so the quotient reads 0.142.
Attach a zero to the 6 to make 60. Seven eights are 56, giving the digit 8 and a remainder of 4, so the quotient reads 0.1428.
Attach a zero to the 4 to make 40. Seven fives are 35, giving the digit 5 and a remainder of 5, so the quotient reads 0.14285.
Attach a zero to the 5 to make 50. Seven sevens are 49, giving the digit 7 and a remainder of 1. That is the number the division began with, so from this point everything repeats.
Because the remainders ran 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5 and then returned to 1, the six digits 142857 must recur for ever, which is what the bar over them records.

Look at what the repeating block does under multiplication: 142857 doubled is 285714 and tripled is 428571, the same six digits in the same cyclic order entered at a different point. That is why 142857 is called a cyclic number, and why every seventh can be read straight off this one block.

common_mistakes: Stopping the division as soon as a digit looks familiar. The block is closed only when the remainder returns to 1, which happens after six digits.
Confusing the two sequences: 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5 are the remainders, while 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7 are the quotient digits.

solution.operation: Set up division and identify pattern length
solution.description: Set up the division of 1 by 13 and note that its period runs to six digits, so exactly six remainders will appear before the cycle closes on itself.

Record the remainders in the order the division throws them up: 1, then 10, 9, 12, 3, 4, and back to 1. Each is ten times the one before it with multiples of 13 removed, so the list is a geometric progression rather than an arbitrary sequence.

Check the block by multiplying it back. The product of 0.076923 and 13 is 0.999999, which is 1 to every place carried, so the digits are right.

examples.problem_statement: Consider the fraction $\frac{1}{19}$ as our first illustration of the method described.

solution.operation: Set up the fraction and note the denominator ends with 9
solution.description: Note that 19 ends in 9, which is the condition for using Ekadhikena Purvena. The digit standing before the 9 is 1, so one more than it, namely 2, is the multiplier for the whole expansion.

solution.operation: Start with the last digit (rightmost) as 1 and multiply by 2 repeatedly
solution.description: Start at the rightmost place with the seed 1 and multiply it by 2. The product 2 is written immediately to its left, so the expansion is built backwards, from the last digit of the period towards the first.
Multiply the 2 just written by 2 to get 4, which takes the third place counting from the right.
Doubling the 4 gives 8, the fourth digit from the right, and there is still no carry to hold.
Doubling 8 gives 16, the first product too large for one place. Write 6 as the fifth digit from the right and hold the 1 as a carry.
Double the 6 just written and add the carried 1, giving 13. Write 3 as the sixth digit and carry 1 forward again.
Double the 3 and add the carry of 1 to get 7. That is the seventh digit, and this time nothing is carried on.
Doubling 7 gives 14, so the eighth digit is 4 and a 1 goes forward as carry.
Double the 4 and add the carry to get 9, the ninth digit, which leaves no carry behind.
Doubling 9 gives 18: write 8 as the tenth digit and carry 1.
Double the 8 and add the carry to get 17, so the eleventh digit is 7 and 1 is carried on.
Double the 7 and add the carry to get 15, putting 5 in the twelfth place with 1 carried.
Double the 5 and add the carry to get 11, so the thirteenth digit is 1 and another 1 is carried.
Double the 1 and add the carry to get 3, the fourteenth digit, with nothing left to carry.
Doubling 3 gives 6, the fifteenth digit, again with no carry.
Doubling 6 gives 12, so the sixteenth digit is 2 and 1 is carried.
Double the 2 and add the carry to get 5, the seventeenth digit, which clears the carry.
Doubling 5 gives 10, so the eighteenth and last digit of the period is 0, with 1 carried into the closing check.

Double the 0 and add the carried 1: the result is 1, the very seed the chain began with. Returning to the seed after eighteen digits is the signal that the period is complete and no further doubling is needed.
Read the digits from left to right, that is in the reverse of the order they were produced, to get the eighteen-digit recurring block 052631578947368421 for one nineteenth.
